blocks.x: SMS 151 · Basic Medical Chemistry · Dept. of Pharmaceutical Chemistry, KNUST

The chemistry of two simple but reactive hydrocarbon families — compounds built around a carbon–carbon double bond (alkenes) or triple bond (alkynes). Their exposed π-electrons make them among the most reactive functional groups in organic and medicinal chemistry.

C=Cthe defining functional group of an alkene — a carbon–carbon double bond, stronger than a single bond but the source of the molecule's reactivity C≡Cthe defining functional group of an alkyne — a carbon–carbon triple bond, linear and 180° at the sp-hybridized carbons C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n−2</sub>general molecular formula for both alkynes and (independently) cyclic/di-unsaturated alkenes
By the end of this topic, you will be able to…

items: 1Name and draw alkenes and alkynes — using IUPAC nomenclature and common (trivial) names, and recognise geometric (cis/trans) isomerism.
2Explain the bonding in alkenes (sp2, trigonal planar, one π bond) and alkynes (sp, linear, two π bonds), and relate hybridization to reactivity and acidity.

3Predict the products of addition reactions — hydrogenation, halogenation, hydrohalogenation, hydration and oxidation — including regiochemistry (Markovnikov's rule) and stereochemistry (syn/anti addition).
4Describe how carbocation stability and mechanism (electrophilic addition, carbocation rearrangement) explain which product forms as the major product.
5Outline preparations of alkenes and alkynes from alkyl halides and vicinal dihalides, and recognise alkenes/alkynes as building blocks of natural products and drugs.

blocks.x: Core definitions

Alkene A hydrocarbon containing at least one carbon–carbon double bond. The two carbons of the double bond are sp2 hybridized (trigonal planar, ~120° bond angles). The double bond is stronger than a C–C single bond, but it is also the source of the molecule's reactivity — the exposed π-electron cloud is attacked by electrophiles.

Alkyne A hydrocarbon containing at least one carbon–carbon triple bond (CnH2n−2). The two carbons of the triple bond are sp hybridized (linear, 180°). A triple bond is one σ bond plus two mutually perpendicular π bonds.

Addition reaction The general reactivity pattern of both families: a reagent A–B adds across the multiple bond, converting π electrons into new σ bonds (rehybridization), with no loss of atoms. General form: –C=C– + A–B → –C(A)–C(B)–.

Markovnikov's Rule "In the ionic addition of an acid (H–X) to the carbon–carbon double bond of an alkene, the hydrogen of the acid attaches itself to the carbon atom which already holds the greater number of hydrogens." (V. W. Markovnikov, 1838–1904) — informally, "them that has, gets."

Alkenes and alkynes are not just laboratory curiosities — they occur throughout nature and medicine: ethylene (a plant hormone), the aphid alarm pheromone 3-methylene-7,11-dimethyl-1,6,10-dodecatriene, the antitumour agents calicheamicin and esperamicin (which use reactive enediyne triple-bond systems), and synthetic alkyne drugs such as pargyline (antihypertensive), parsalmide (analgesic), and mestranol (a component of oral contraceptives).
Alkane (C–C, sp<sup>3</sup>)→ Alkene (C=C, sp<sup>2</sup>)→ Alkyne (C≡C, sp)

blocks.x: Orbital theory
The number of hybrid orbitals a carbon atom uses depends on how many σ-bonding partners it has — and this, in turn, dictates molecular geometry.
Carbon's valence configuration

The valence shell electron configuration of carbon is 2s2, 2px1, 2py1, 2pz0. To explain carbon's four equivalent bonds (as in methane and carbon tetrachloride, both perfectly tetrahedral), one 2s electron is promoted to the empty 2pz orbital, and the 2s + three 2p orbitals mix (hybridize).
sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbitals — alkanes

The 2s orbital combines with all three 2p orbitals to give four equivalent sp3 hybrid orbitals, each 25% s and 75% p character. These orient tetrahedrally, 109.5° apart — the geometry of methane, and of every sp3 carbon in an alkane chain. The total number of orbitals is conserved: 1 s + 3 p in → 4 sp3 out.
sp<sup>2</sup> hybrid orbitals — alkenes

A carbon involved in a double bond has only three σ-bonding partners, so it needs only three hybrid orbitals. The 2s orbital mixes with two of the three 2p orbitals to give three sp2 hybrid orbitals (trigonal planar, 120° apart), leaving one p orbital unused and unhybridized, perpendicular to the sp2 plane.

Two sp2 carbons join through a sigma (σ) bond (head-on overlap of sp2 orbitals) plus a pi (π) bond (sideways overlap of the two leftover p orbitals, above and below the molecular plane). Together, σ + π = the C=C double bond.
sp hybrid orbitals — alkynes

A carbon with only two σ-bonding partners needs only two hybrid orbitals. The 2s orbital mixes with one 2p orbital to give two sp hybrid orbitals, directed 180° from each other (linear geometry) — and two p orbitals remain unused on each sp carbon.

The two leftover, mutually perpendicular p orbitals on each of the two sp carbons overlap sideways to form two π bonds, in addition to the sp–sp σ bond. A triple bond = 1 σ + 2 π bonds, giving the linear H–C≡C–H geometry of acetylene.
Hybridization at a glance
Why the alkynyl C–H bond is unusually acidic

An sp orbital has more s character (50%) than sp2 (33%) or sp3 (25%). Because s orbitals sit closer to the nucleus than p orbitals, electrons in an sp orbital are held closer to the carbon nucleus — making an sp carbon more electronegative than sp2 or sp3 carbon. This is why the terminal alkynyl C–H bond is more polar than an alkane or alkene C–H bond, and why terminal alkynes can be deprotonated by sufficiently strong bases (see Alkyne Structure & Properties). This same restricted π-bond rotation (geometric isomerism) that is possible for alkenes is not possible for alkanes or alkynes.
Nomenclature & physical chemistry
Alkenes involve a carbon–carbon double bond. This double bond is stronger than a single bond, but it is also the source of the reactivity of these molecules.
IUPAC nomenclature
Replace the alkane suffix –ane with –ene. A locant number gives the position of the double bond (lowest possible number).
Trivial names of alkenyl groups
Methylene
The =CH2 group, e.g. methylenecyclohexane, CH2=<cyclohexane ring>.
Vinyl
The CH2=CH– group, e.g. vinyl chloride, CH2=CHCl (the monomer of PVC).
Allyl
The CH2=CH–CH2– group, e.g. allyl bromide, CH2=CH–CH2Br.
Properties

Because of the exposed π electrons in alkenes, there is some slight interaction with water molecules — absent in alkanes. Alkenes are therefore slightly more soluble in water than alkanes, even though alkenes are still considered nonpolar overall. Other physical properties, e.g. boiling point, are essentially identical to their alkane parents.
Preparation of alkenes

Alkenes are commonly made by elimination reactions — of alkyl halides (dehydrohalogenation, with a base such as Na+ −OCH2CH3, warm) or of alcohols (dehydration). Whether the substrate is 1°, 2° or 3°, mixtures of alkene products typically result.
2-bromopentane → trans-2-pentene (51%, major) + cis-2-pentene (18%) + 1-pentene (31%)Na<sup>+ −</sup>OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, warm
cis / trans (geometric) isomerism

Because the C=C π bond restricts free rotation, alkenes bearing two different substituents on each double-bond carbon can exist as distinct, non-interconvertible cis and trans isomers — e.g. 1-bromopropene can be drawn with both substituted groups (CH3 and Br) on the same side (cis) or on opposite sides (trans) of the double bond. Unlike a C–C single bond, the C=C double bond cannot rotate without breaking the π bond.
Conjugation

Sequential double-bond/single-bond patterns (e.g. CH2=CH–CH=CH–CH3) are said to be conjugated, and conjugated dienes have increased stability compared with an isolated (non-conjugated) diene of the same formula, e.g. CH2=CH–CH2–CH=CH2. Double bonds can also be conjugated within a ring, e.g. 1,3-cyclohexadiene.
Benzene & aromaticity

Take conjugation to its limit: three alternating double bonds within a six-membered ring gives benzene — a compound so stabilised by aromaticity that it behaves fundamentally differently from an ordinary alkene.
Benzene can react with Br2, but only in the presence of a catalyst (FeBr3) — and critically, the reaction is a substitution, not an addition:
C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> (colourless) + Br<sub>2</sub> (red) → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br + HBr (colourless)FeBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst

Aromatic compounds like benzene preserve their ring of conjugated π electrons by substituting one H for Br rather than adding Br2 across a double bond, because addition would destroy the aromatic stabilisation. Compounds that are not aromatic are called aliphatic (a term that originally referred to their smell).

sections.title: Electrophilic addition to a double bond

blocks.x: Reactivity of the C=C double bond
The double bond is the source of alkene reactivity. Its main type of reaction is addition: reagents add across the π bond, the carbons rehybridize from sp2 to sp3, and no atoms are lost.
Electrophilic addition to a double bond

Because the π bond is a region of exposed, loosely-held electron density, alkenes react as nucleophiles toward electrophiles (X+–Y or polarized X–Y). A two-step mechanism is typical: (1) the π bond attacks the electrophile, forming a carbocation intermediate; (2) the nucleophile (Y−) attacks the carbocation. Intermediates are formed during a reaction but are not products.
Hydrogenation (reduction)
R–CH=CH–R + H<sub>2</sub> → R–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–RPt, Pd or Ni catalyst (also PtO<sub>2</sub>; sometimes Ru, Rh, Re)

Both H atoms are delivered to the same face of the double bond from the metal surface — a syn-addition, and it is stereospecific. This is the basis of industrial hydrogenation of fats/oils to margarine. Note: hydrogenation of alkenes is a reduction.
Halogenation (addition of Br<sub>2</sub> / Cl<sub>2</sub>)
R–CH=CH–R + Br<sub>2</sub> → R–CHBr–CHBr–RCCl<sub>4</sub> or CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> solvent

Mechanism: the alkene's π electrons polarize the approaching Br–Br bond (δ+/δ−), then attack the electrophilic bromine to form a cyclic bromonium ion and release Br− (the slow step). The bromide ion then attacks the bromonium ion from the opposite face (backside attack), giving anti-addition — stereospecific, with the two new C–Br bonds trans to each other.
Hydrohalogenation (H–X) & Markovnikov's rule
Adding an unsymmetrical reagent like HBr to an unsymmetrical alkene, e.g. 2-methylpropene, can give two different constitutional isomers:
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH<sub>2</sub> + HBr → (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–Br (major, tert-alkyl bromide) + (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH–CH<sub>2</sub>Br (minor)

Markovnikov's rule: the H of H–X attaches to the carbon that already has the greater number of hydrogens; conversely, the halide (X−) ends up on the more highly substituted carbon (the carbon with more alkyl groups attached). This reaction is regioselective — one product forms in larger amount than the other (as opposed to regiospecific, where only one product forms, 100%).
Mechanism & carbocation stability

Step 1 (slow): the alkene π bond attacks H+ (the electrophile), generating a carbocation. Protonation occurs so as to give the more stable (more substituted) carbocation — e.g. a secondary carbocation forms preferentially over a primary one, because alkyl groups are electron-donating and stabilise the positive charge (hyperconjugation and induction).
Step 2 (fast): the nucleophile (Br−) attacks the carbocation to give the major, Markovnikov product.

By contrast, if H+ instead added to give a primary carbocation (the anti-Markovnikov pathway), that higher-energy intermediate would form much more slowly, so the pathway through it contributes only a minor amount of product. Stability order of carbocations: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl.
Carbocation rearrangements

If the initially-formed carbocation can rearrange (by a 1,2-hydride or 1,2-methyl shift) to a more stable carbocation, it will — and the major product reflects this rearranged skeleton, not the original connectivity. For example, addition of HCl to 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene gives a rearranged tertiary-chloride major product (via hydride shift from a secondary to a more stable tertiary carbocation) alongside a minor, non-rearranged product.
Anti-Markovnikov addition (peroxide effect)

Under radical conditions (e.g. HBr with peroxides/O2 present), addition proceeds through a bromine radical mechanism instead of a carbocation mechanism. The radical adds first to give the more stable radical (again favouring the more substituted carbon for the radical), which places Br on the less substituted carbon — the anti-Markovnikov orientation. This only occurs for HBr (not HCl or HI) under radical-initiating conditions.
Addition of sulfuric acid
R–CH=CH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (cold, conc.) → R–CH(OSO<sub>3</sub>H)–CH<sub>3</sub> (an alkyl hydrogen sulfate)

Cold, concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> adds across the double bond via the same electrophilic (Markovnikov) mechanism as HX addition, giving an alkyl hydrogen sulfate. Hydrolysis of this intermediate is a classic industrial route to alcohols.
Addition of water (hydration)
R–CH=CH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → R–CH(OH)–CH<sub>3</sub>H<sup>+</sup> catalyst
Acid-catalysed hydration proceeds through the same carbocation mechanism, so it also follows Markovnikov orientation — the OH ends up on the more substituted carbon.
Oxidation
The outcome of KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidation depends sharply on conditions:
Syn-dihydroxylation via a cyclic epoxide/manganate ester intermediate → a 1,2-diol (glycol), with both new OH groups on the same face.
Hot, concentrated KMnO<sub>4</sub> HARSH
Oxidative cleavage of the C=C bond entirely → aldehydes, ketones, or carboxylic acids, depending on the substitution pattern at each alkene carbon (a terminal =CH2 is oxidised all the way to CO2).
The triple bond
Alkynes (C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n−2</sub>) contain a carbon–carbon triple bond: one σ bond plus two π bonds, giving linear, 180° geometry at the sp carbons.
Ethyne (acetylene)
C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub> H–C≡C–H (sp ⇒ linear, 180°)
Common name: acetylene. IUPAC name: ethyne. The next member, C3H4 (CH3C≡CH), is propyne (common name: methylacetylene).
Nomenclature
Common names: "alkylacetylene" (name each substituent + "acetylene"), e.g. CH3CH2C≡CCH3 = ethylmethylacetylene.

IUPAC: the parent chain is the longest continuous carbon chain that contains the triple bond. Drop the alkane suffix –ane, add –yne, and give the lowest possible locant for the triple bond, e.g. CH3CH2C≡CCH3 = 2-pentyne.
Terminal alkynes have the triple bond at the very end of the chain, e.g. CH3CH2C≡CH = 1-butyne (ethylacetylene); HC≡C–CH(CH3)–CH2CH3 = 3-methyl-1-pentyne (sec-butylacetylene).
Properties
Bulk properties
Weakly or non-polar overall, no hydrogen bonding possible, relatively low melting/boiling points, and water-insoluble — broadly similar to alkanes and alkenes.
C–H bond polarity

The sp-hybridized carbon has 50% s character (orbitals closer to the nucleus), making it more electronegative than sp2/sp3 carbon — so the terminal alkynyl C–H bond is more polar than an alkane or alkene C–H.
Terminal alkynes as (very) weak acids

Because of the increased C–H polarity, terminal alkynes can lose that hydrogen to a sufficiently strong base, forming an acetylide ion (RC≡C−). They are nonetheless weaker acids than water. Alkanes and (internal) alkenes do not react under these conditions.
CH<sub>3</sub>C≡CH + Na<sup>+ −</sup>NH<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>C≡C<sup>−</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> + NH<sub>3</sub>liquid NH<sub>3</sub>

Relative acid strength: CH4 < NH3 < HC≡CH < ROH < H2O < HF. Because water is a stronger acid than a terminal alkyne, hydroxide is too weak a base to deprotonate an alkyne — HC≡CH + NaOH → NR (no reaction). But amide ion (NH2−, the conjugate base of the much weaker acid NH3) is a strong enough base to deprotonate a terminal alkyne readily.
Alkynes in nature

Naturally-occurring alkynes are rare. Examples: capillin (fungicidal activity) and ichthyothereol (a convulsant used by Amazon Indians for poisoned arrowheads). A class of naturally occurring compounds called enediynes have powerful antibiotic and anticancer properties — they contain a nine- or ten-membered ring with two triple bonds separated by a double bond; examples include calicheamicin and esperamicin, potent antitumour agents derived from bacteria. Some enediynes are currently in clinical trials.
Alkyne functional groups in medicines
Unlike the natural enediynes above, these drugs exist only because chemists have synthesised them — they are not naturally occurring compounds.
Making & using the triple bond
Alkynes are built from alkyl dihalides or by coupling acetylide anions, and then undergo a well-defined set of seven reaction types.
Dehydrohalogenation of vicinal dihalides

A vicinal dihalide (from halogenating an alkene) undergoes double elimination: the first equivalent of strong base (KOH) gives a vinyl halide, and a second equivalent (KOH, heat, or NaNH2) removes the second HX to give the alkyne.
alkene →X<sub>2</sub> vicinal dihalide →1. KOH 2. NaNH<sub>2</sub> alkyne
CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub> →Br<sub>2</sub> CH<sub>3</sub>CHBr–CH<sub>2</sub>Br →1. KOH 2. NaNH<sub>2</sub> CH<sub>3</sub>C≡CH
Equivalently, 2 KOH with heat can convert a vicinal dihalide directly to the alkyne in one pot.
Coupling of metal acetylides with 1°/CH<sub>3</sub> alkyl halides
R–C≡C<sup>−</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> + R′–X → R–C≡C–R′ + NaXS<sub>N</sub>2
The acetylide ion is a strong nucleophile and attacks the alkyl halide in an SN2 reaction. This only works when R′X is a primary (1°) or methyl halide — e.g. CH3C≡C−Li+ + CH3CH2Br → CH3C≡CCH2CH3.

If R′X is instead a tertiary (3°) alkyl halide, the bulky acetylide ion is too hindered and too basic to perform SN2 substitution; instead it acts as a base and promotes E2 elimination, regenerating an alkene from the halide plus the original neutral alkyne (no new C–C bond forms).
The seven classes of alkyne reactions
Addition of hydrogen
–C≡C– + 2 H<sub>2</sub> → –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– (alkane)Ni, Pt, or Pd
Full reduction over Ni/Pt/Pd gives the alkane directly. To stop cleanly at the alkene stage, two selective catalysts are used, each with different stereochemistry:
Anti-addition → the trans-alkene (dissolving-metal reduction, radical-anion mechanism).
H<sub>2</sub>, Pd–C, Lindlar catalyst
Syn-addition → the cis-alkene (Lindlar = Pd poisoned with Pb/quinoline to stop at the alkene).
E.g. CH<sub>3</sub>C≡CCH<sub>3</sub> → trans-2-butene (Na/NH<sub>3</sub>) or cis-2-butene (Lindlar).
Addition of halogens (X<sub>2</sub>)
CH<sub>3</sub>C≡CH + Br<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CBr=CHBr →+ Br<sub>2</sub> CH<sub>3</sub>CBr<sub>2</sub>–CHBr<sub>2</sub>
One equivalent of X<sub>2</sub> gives a dihaloalkene; a second equivalent adds again to give the tetrahalide, exactly analogous to alkene halogenation but occurring twice.
Addition of hydrogen halides (HX)
CH<sub>3</sub>C≡CH + HCl → CH<sub>3</sub>CCl=CH<sub>2</sub> →+ HCl CH<sub>3</sub>CCl<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub>

HX = HI, HBr or HCl; addition follows Markovnikov orientation at each step (H to the carbon with more H's already), and a second equivalent can add to give a geminal dihalide (both halogens on the same carbon).
Addition of water (hydration)
–C≡C– + H<sub>2</sub>O → [enol, –CH=C(OH)–] → –CH<sub>2</sub>–C(=O)–H<sup>+</sup>, HgO catalyst (Markovnikov orientation)

Hydration first gives an unstable enol (a C=C with an OH on one of the double-bond carbons), which immediately undergoes keto-enol tautomerism to the far more stable carbonyl (ketone) form. Markovnikov orientation places the new C=O on the more substituted carbon.
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C≡CH (1-butyne) + H<sub>2</sub>O → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C(=O)CH<sub>3</sub> (2-butanone)H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, HgO
Terminal alkynes as acids
CH<sub>3</sub>C≡CH + Na → CH<sub>3</sub>C≡C<sup>−</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> + ½ H<sub>2</sub>↑(a) with active metals
CH<sub>3</sub>C≡CH + CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr → CH<sub>4</sub> + CH<sub>3</sub>C≡CMgBr(b) with strong bases (Grignard reagents)

Only terminal alkynes react this way. As shown above, the terminal alkyne is a stronger acid (SA) than the methane (WA) or ammonia produced — the reaction proceeds because the acid on the left is always stronger than the conjugate acid formed on the right.
Test with silver nitrate (Ag<sup>+</sup>)
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C≡CH + AgNO<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C≡C–Ag↓ (precipitate)
CH<sub>3</sub>C≡CCH<sub>3</sub> + AgNO<sub>3</sub> → NR (not terminal — no reaction)
Only terminal alkynes form the insoluble silver acetylide precipitate. Formation of a precipitate is therefore a qualitative test for terminal alkynes.
Oxidative cleavage
R–C≡C–R′ → RCOOH + HOOCR′hot KMnO<sub>4</sub>, OR O<sub>3</sub> then Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O

Hot KMnO4 or ozonolysis (O3, then reductive workup with Zn/H2O) completely cleaves the triple bond, oxidising each carbon to a carboxylic acid. Example: CH3C≡CH + hot KMnO4 → CH3COOH + CO2 (a terminal ≡CH carbon is oxidised all the way to CO2). A symmetric internal alkyne like CH3C≡CCH3 gives 2 equivalents of CH3COOH.
